notes.body: The chapter's whole test is 'which speech is praiseworthy?' — and the answer turns on where speech begins. Picture the fool: his tongue fires first, blurting from raw impulse, and his heart scrambles afterward to justify whatever fell out. The wise man runs it backwards — truth reaches the heart first, gets weighed against a higher measure, and only then is the tongue permitted to speak. So 'correct' speech isn't clever speech; it's speech that passed through the heart before it passed the lips.
notes.quote: And speech is the same — praiseworthy and condemnable

notes.body: 'The outward in plain view, the inward a hidden green' isn't just poetry — it's a preservation strategy. Think of the visible world — the seasons, the fixed paths of the stars, the law, the rituals — as a hard shell wrapped around a fragile inner truth. Left exposed, egos would seize and twist that truth, so it's sealed inside the outer architecture; civilizations rise and fall but the shell keeps carrying the essence across time. The catch: you can't crack the shell by cleverness alone — that's why the path needs an appointed guide.
notes.anchor: outward in view, inward a hidden green
notes.quote: the outward of His way a thing in plain view, and the inward a hidden green

notes.body: Notice the elder just watches and waits instead of jumping in to correct the debate. His reason: pouring deep truth into an unready heart doesn't merely waste effort — it does harm, because that person weaponizes the knowledge for status. So what is he actually listening for? The seeking itself. People drift toward comfort by default, so the hard, unrewarded work of genuinely hunting for an answer is the visible trace of a higher prompting — which is why 'the one who is hunting a thing is already close to finding it.'
notes.anchor: the one hunting is already close to finding
notes.quote: the one who is hunting a thing is already close to finding it

notes.body: Here's one to put to your reading partner. The stranger sorts all speech by its origin — speech that begins from God and calls toward Him, versus speech that begins from appetite and calls somewhere else. Ask them: the last thing you found yourself really persuaded by this week — which spring was it drawn from?
notes.anchor: speech from God vs speech from appetite
